speaker: Jennifer Doudna
title: Editing Your DNA, with Nobel Prize Winner Dr. Jennifer Doudna
question: In in vivo gene editing, what actually makes delivering therapies to complex organs like the brain so difficult?
guest: We have many different kinds of cells in our bodies, and even within one organ like our brain, many cell types are required to form it. When a disease like Alzheimer's affects the brain, it primarily affects only some of those cells, not all of them. Ideally, you want to get the genome editor into just those cells where a DNA change helps the patient without bothering other cells in the body. Doing that is tricky because the cells are all growing together, so you need a chemical mechanism to distinguish one cell type from another. Cells often have surface zip code molecules marking different cell types, but science is still figuring out which zip codes go with which cell type. Even once we know that, the challenge is recognizing one specific set of surface molecules while ignoring all others. Viruses are very good at that, so one major inspiration in delivery is studying how viruses do that recognition and delivery, and repurposing it to carry our CRISPR cargo instead.

points.core: Diseases often affect only a subset of intermingled cells inside organs.
points.note: Accept: organs contain mixed cell populations where pathology hits specific cell types, editing must reach only affected cells without disturbing neighboring healthy cells. Do not credit: generic statements that the brain is complex or hard to reach.

points.note: Accept: unknown cell-surface zip codes, incomplete catalog of surface receptors or epitopes distinguishing specific cell types. Do not credit: citing the blood-brain barrier alone without cell-surface identification.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Delivering in vivo gene-editing therapies to organs like the brain is hard mainly because of biological barriers and cellular diversity. The blood-brain barrier blocks most large molecules—including viral vectors and lipid nanoparticles—from crossing out of the bloodstream, so systemic dosing rarely reaches neurons efficiently. Direct injection helps but spreads poorly, since editing machinery diffuses only short distances through dense tissue, leaving much of the organ untouched.

The brain is also made of many distinct, intermixed cell types (neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes), and most are post-mitotic, which limits certain editing approaches that rely on cell division. Achieving the right targeting—hitting the intended cells without affecting others—is difficult, and immune responses to viral capsids or Cas proteins can reduce efficacy or cause inflammation.

Dosing and scale matter too: the brain is large, and getting enough editing reagent to enough cells, at sustained levels, without toxicity is a hard balance. Finally, you can't easily sample or correct edits once delivered, so precision, durability, and safety must be right the first time.

points.why: The response describes intermixed cell types and selective targeting but never explains that disease preferentially affects a subset of those cells.
The response omits the incomplete mapping of cell-type-specific surface markers.
The response calls for targeting intended cells without describing how a delivery vehicle would selectively recognize their surface molecules.
The response mentions viral vectors and capsids in connection with delivery barriers and immune responses but omits repurposing viral cell recognition to carry editing cargo.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Delivering gene-editing therapies into complex organs like the brain requires overcoming stacked vascular, physical, and cellular barriers. Systemically injected carriers are heavily sequestered by the liver and cleared by the immune system, while the blood-brain barrier tightly blocks large macromolecules, standard viral vectors, and lipid nanoparticles from exiting blood vessels. Bypassing circulation via direct intracranial injection solves access only locally, because dense tissue and extracellular matrix restrict diffusion across a large human brain. Meanwhile, CRISPR nucleases, base editors, and prime editors are bulky multi-component cargoes that exceed or strain the small packaging limit of adeno-associated viruses and complicate nanoparticle formulation. Even after reaching brain tissue, vehicles must selectively target disease-relevant subtypes among dozens of intermingled neurons and glia, escape endosomes, and enter the nuclei of non-dividing cells. Finally, editor expression must be brief enough to prevent cumulative off-target DNA cuts, neuroinflammation, and immune attacks against foreign bacterial proteins, yet viral vectors persist long-term while transient non-viral nanoparticles still distribute poorly beyond the injection site.

points.why: The response identifies disease-relevant cell subtypes within a mixed population and explicitly calls for selectively targeting them.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Delivering gene-editing therapies to the brain is hard mainly because of biological barriers and the organ's complexity. The blood-brain barrier blocks most large molecules and delivery vehicles—like adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), lipid nanoparticles, or the editing machinery itself—from crossing out of the bloodstream into neural tissue. Neurons are post-mitotic (non-dividing), which limits some editing approaches and makes them hard to reach and replace. The brain is also extraordinarily heterogeneous: many distinct cell types sit in precise circuits, so you often need to edit specific populations without disturbing others, and achieving broad, even distribution across such a large, densely packed structure is difficult. Direct injection reaches only local regions and is invasive, while systemic delivery struggles to concentrate enough dose in the right place. Immune responses against viral vectors or Cas proteins can reduce efficacy and prevent re-dosing. Finally, the stakes raise the bar: off-target edits or inflammation in irreplaceable neural tissue carry serious, often irreversible consequences, so both precision and safety thresholds are far more demanding than in regenerating tissues like liver.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Delivering in vivo gene-editing therapies to complex organs like the brain is difficult because multiple biological and engineering barriers compound one another. First, the blood-brain barrier—a tightly sealed network of specialized endothelial cells—blocks large therapeutic cargoes from crossing from the bloodstream into neural tissue. Even when vectors bypass this barrier or are injected directly, they must navigate a dense extracellular matrix to reach deep, widespread structures rather than staying localized near the injection site. Meanwhile, systemically administered nanoparticles and viral vectors are heavily sequestered by the liver before reaching target organs. Cargo size adds another hurdle: editing systems such as CRISPR-Cas9, base editors, and prime editors are bulky, often exceeding the packaging limits of standard adeno-associated viruses. Finally, the brain’s cellular diversity demands precise targeting of specific cell types—like particular neurons or glia—without triggering neuroinflammation or immune responses against the delivery vehicle or bacterial-derived editing enzymes, which also complicates repeat dosing.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An in vivo gene editor has to reach enough of the right cells and get inside them in working form. In the brain, the blood–brain barrier keeps most editing cargo and delivery vehicles out of brain tissue after an IV dose. Injecting directly into the brain bypasses that barrier, but the dose may spread only a short distance from the injection site. That matters when the cells that need treatment are scattered across multiple regions.

Even after reaching the right region, the editor has to enter the intended cell type, escape the compartments that can trap or degrade it after uptake, and reach the nucleus. Some delivery vehicles have limited room for the editing machinery, and immune responses can limit the dose or make repeat dosing difficult. The central challenge is getting enough editing across the cells that drive the disease while keeping exposure elsewhere low.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A gene editor has to reach the right cells and get inside them. In the brain, the blood–brain barrier keeps most large molecules and delivery particles in the bloodstream. Injecting a therapy directly into brain tissue can bypass that barrier, but the dose may stay near the injection site while the cells that need treatment are spread across several regions.

Even when the editor reaches the right region, neighboring neurons and support cells can take it up at different rates. A cell may also trap the cargo in an internal compartment and break it down before the editor reaches DNA in the nucleus. Increasing the dose can expose more cells, but it can also trigger inflammation or increase editing in unintended cells. The challenge is to edit enough of the cells that drive the disease at a dose the patient can tolerate.
